tip.title: Pay cash for today's small purchases
tip.why: How you pay changes how much you are willing to spend. Prelec and Simester (Marketing Letters, 2001) ran a sealed-bid auction for Boston Celtics tickets with MBA students, telling half they would pay in cash and half by credit card. The credit-card group bid roughly twice as much: average bids of about $61 against about $29 for cash. The authors' reading is that a card dulls the felt cost of parting with money, which is exactly what you want to feel on a Saturday full of small, optional spending.
how: Before you leave the house, take out a set amount of cash for the day, say $40, and leave the cards in a drawer or deep in your bag.
Use only that cash for coffee, lunch, groceries and anything else unplanned; when it is gone, you are done spending for the day.
Tonight, count what is left and write down the one purchase you skipped because handing over bills felt different.
tip.ask: What would you have bought today if the money had felt less real?

points: The S&P 500 dropped 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive decline and more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93, so the index and the Dow both closed in correction territory. The Dow fell 949.73 points (1.9%) to 48,147.33 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points (5.3%) to 22,617.73, turning negative for 2026 (down 2.7%), while the VIX closed at 35.89. For the week the S&P 500 lost 8.61%, the Nasdaq 10.02% (its steepest weekly drop since 2020), the Dow 8.02% and the Russell 2000 7.48%; the S&P 500 is now up only about 0.9% for the year.

Semiconductors led the selling. Nvidia fell 14%, its worst day since the DeepSeek selloff, after Reuters reported the SEC is examining the company's accounting, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost 10.7%. Intel gave back Thursday's gain on its first external 18A foundry customer, falling 7.97% to $51.28 (from $55.72) as the chip selloff spread; TradingKey also cited a reported 25% cut in Nvidia's Intel stake, and a law firm announced a class action against Intel the same day. Anthropic's Thursday IPO pop did nothing to stop the rout: CNBC framed Friday's selloff as the AI trade failing to revive after the debut.

Tesla dropped 7.64% to $345.82 as analysts questioned the benefit of the reported merger with SpaceX, even though HSBC upgraded the stock to Hold from Reduce and lifted its target to $359 from $157, saying the potential combination shifts the valuation debate toward a possible acquisition price. SpaceX fell 7.69% to $127.79, back below its IPO price, as TipRanks tied the drop to new problems with its planned $74 billion AI infrastructure investment and a Cameron County, Texas vote against a hearing on a tax break for a $24 billion project; Apollo and Goldman Sachs priced a $44 billion SpaceX GPU financing deal the same day.

Money moved into Treasuries: the 10-year yield fell about 7 basis points to roughly 4.97% as investors sought safe havens ahead of a speech by Fed Governor Christopher Waller, who said a half-point December hike may be necessary; CME FedWatch put the odds of at least a quarter-point hike in December at 98.7%. After the close, Bloomberg and Reuters reported CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, sending Zscaler up roughly 17% to 18% in extended trading and CrowdStrike down about 8%.

pick.name: Zscaler
pick.theme: Takeover target: cloud-security vendor Zscaler jumped 17% to 18% after hours Friday on Bloomberg and Reuters reports that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy it, after closing the regular session down 5.3% at $194.82
pick.what: Zscaler sells cloud-delivered security. Its Zero Trust Exchange routes a company's internet and private-application traffic through Zscaler's own data centers, where it inspects it and enforces policy, replacing on-premises firewalls and VPNs; the core products are Zscaler Internet Access (secure web gateway) and Zscaler Private Access (zero-trust access to internal apps), plus data-protection, cloud-workload and AI-security add-ons. Revenue is almost entirely subscription, sold to large enterprises and governments. The company held a 2026 Investor Day on Oct. 6 and reaffirmed guidance; it trades on Nasdaq as ZS with a market value of roughly $32 billion to $33.5 billion at Friday's close.
pick.why: Zscaler is in play. After Friday's close, Bloomberg and Reuters reported that CrowdStrike is negotiating to acquire the company; neither side has confirmed the talks and Reuters said no deal is guaranteed. ZS rose about 17% to 18% in extended trading (quotes ranged from about $226 to $239) from a regular-session close of $194.82, down $10.89 (5.3%) on a day the Nasdaq fell 5.3%; CrowdStrike fell about 8% after hours. Any agreed price would need a premium to the roughly $33.5 billion market value, and the stock had already been swinging hard: Investing.com shows a Nov. 17 close of $180.99 while Yahoo's prior close for Nov. 19 was $205.71. Before the report, analysts were constructive: TipRanks lists a Strong Buy consensus from 36 analysts (30 Buy, 6 Hold, 0 Sell) with a $239.50 average target, and StockAnalysis (47 analysts polled by S&P Global) rates it Buy with a $235.19 average target; Truist reiterated Buy with a $250 target on Nov. 16, and BofA ($285) and Citi ($260) recently raised targets. The stock is down about 13% in 2026, so the question for research is whether a deal happens, at what price, and what the stock is worth on its own if talks collapse. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: Merger-arbitrage risk dominates. The talks are unconfirmed and could end without a deal, in which case the after-hours gain would likely reverse and the stock would trade back on fundamentals in a market that just punished software and AI names hard. A CrowdStrike deal would be enormous (one report put the combined value near $265 billion) and would face antitrust review and CrowdStrike shareholder pushback, given CRWD fell 8% on the report; a stock-funded deal would also tie ZS holders to CRWD's price. If a deal is agreed, the upside is capped at the takeout price. Fundamentally, Zscaler competes with Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, Cloudflare, Netskope and Microsoft in secure access, and its growth has been decelerating as it scales. Data caveats: the 52-week high and a full month of daily closes could not be retrieved in this session, and sources disagree on several recent closes (Nov. 17 is shown as $180.99 by Investing.com and $185.19 elsewhere).

btc.summary: Cowen posted twice in one day: a 25-minute video Friday morning on bitcoin losing a round-number level it had defended all year, and a 22-minute follow-up Friday night titled Bitcoin: The Lower Low, both recorded around the opening of his first Into the Cryptoverse conference. The title revives his 2022 framing: bitcoin has now printed a lower low beneath the floor it held since the summer, which is the capitulation outcome he had been flagging for November, and the videos weigh the odds of a sharp relief bounce against a further slide into December and January, the window he has called the most vulnerable. His descriptions carry no chapter list, so the detail comes from his recent material: he treats on-chain risk below one tenth and a drop under realized price as the markers of past bottoms, neither of which he says has been reached, and he still frames this as an equities-led selloff in which bitcoin follows the Nasdaq rather than leads it. Viewers in his comments read the new low as vindication of his year-long call for a fourth-quarter low; he has not yet said the low is in.

brief.lede: UN talks end with a 2028 target for rules on autonomous weapons as NIOSH opens the first federal humanoid-safety docket, and ABB weighs a robotics listing. Nvidia fell 14% on a report that the SEC is examining its accounting, dragging the S&P 500 into a correction, while bitcoin broke $60,000 and SpaceX flew USSF-317 on a day its stock fell below its IPO price.

articles.title: Regulators come at humanoids from two directions
body: Humanoid robots landed in front of regulators on two continents this week, for very different reasons. In Geneva, talks under the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons ended early on Saturday, Nov 21, with states agreeing to work toward rules on lethal autonomous weapons **by 2028** but stopping short of launching formal treaty negotiations. Reuters reported that the United States and Russia opposed binding rules; the final mandate uses the word "elaborate" rather than "negotiate", which leaves open whether anything that emerges will bind anyone.

The outcome disappointed the countries that wanted a treaty. Seven states, including Brazil, Austria and Mexico, had proposed formal negotiations on a binding instrument, and UN Secretary-General António Guterres had set 2026 as the deadline to begin them; that deadline has now passed. Campaigners say treaty supporters may now try to route around the consensus-based Geneva forum through the UN General Assembly.

The humanoid angle is no longer hypothetical: at least one US maker holds a Pentagon test contract for a bipedal platform, so rules elaborated by 2028 would arrive just as the first military humanoids move from prototypes toward procurement. The Geneva result mostly buys time; the next two years decide whether limits on machine autonomy become law or guidance.

In the United States, a safety agency is asking a narrower question: how humanoids share a workplace with people. The CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health has posted a request for information from its Center for Occupational Robotics Research, scheduled for Federal Register publication on Monday, Nov 23. It asks what tasks humanoid robots are likely to perform, how their risks and benefits differ from other robots, how they affect workers' awareness, trust, workload and training, and what tests or measures are needed to assess their safety under realistic working conditions. Comments are due **Feb 22, 2027** under docket CDC-2026-1882, and the notice says it is information-gathering only and proposes no regulation.

For anyone building or deploying humanoids, the NIOSH docket is the more actionable item. It is the first federal attempt at a humanoid-specific research agenda, and the questions it poses are the ones industrial customers such as GXO and GlobalFoundries are already asking before letting a biped near a line. It also lands days after Apptronik's reinforcement-learning lead argued publicly that humanoid safety is "wildly under studied". Companies with field data on falls, contact forces and near misses have until February to put it on the record, and the ones that do will have a hand in writing the test methods they are later measured against.

articles.title: ABB weighs a robotics IPO as data vendors raise
body: ABB is considering a stock-market listing of its robotics unit if it cannot rescue the **$5.4 billion** sale to SoftBank that China blocked earlier this month, Reuters reported on Friday, Nov 20, citing two people familiar with the matter. The first preference on both sides is still to save the deal, possibly by carving out the Chinese business, about 30 percent of the unit, and selling it to a Chinese buyer or listing it there. If that fails, ABB would spin the division off or sell it to another party.

Beijing's objection, according to the report, was SoftBank's ties to Western companies including OpenAI and the risk that sensitive robotics data could end up in the United States. It is the second large deal China has blocked this year on similar grounds, after ordering Meta to unwind its purchase of Manus in April. For SoftBank, which also led Agile Robots' $500 million round this month, losing ABB would remove the hardware base it wanted under its physical-AI ambitions.

Money is flowing to the data layer at the same time. Humyn Labs, founded in Bengaluru in February 2026 by Manish Agarwal and Ishank Gupta, raised a **$47 million** Series A, TechCrunch reported on Nov 18: $26 million in equity led by Accel and $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with Trifecta Capital participating and Prosus Ventures also in the round according to one account. The company films people doing physical work in factories, warehouses, farms and homes and sells the footage to US robotics developers as training data. It says it passed $50 million in annualized revenue within six months, a company figure nobody has audited, and will use the money to expand in Brazil, South Korea and India.

Taken together, the week shows two bets on where value in embodied AI will sit: incumbents with installed bases and China exposure, and data vendors selling human video as training fuel. The data bet is the faster moving; Nvidia's GR00T 2 was trained on 100,000 hours of human video, and companies like Humyn exist to supply the next 100,000. The ABB decision is the one to watch, because a listing would give public investors a second way, after Agility, to own robotics directly, and because the Chinese carve-out would set a template for every cross-border robotics deal that follows.

articles.title: Nvidia probe report pushes the S&P 500 into a correction
body: The week ended with the worst session of the selloff. The S&P 500 fell 3.70% on Friday to **6,910.39**, its seventh straight loss, and closed more than 10% below its October 6 record, the usual threshold for a correction. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73 and the Dow lost 949.73 points to 48,147.33. For the week the S&P 500 shed 8.6%, the Nasdaq 10.0% and the Dow about 8%, its worst week since March 2020.

The trigger was a Reuters report, citing two people briefed on the matter, that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. Reuters could not learn when the inquiry began or which practices are involved, and the SEC declined to comment; the Wall Street Journal had reported the probe's existence on November 17 without saying what it covered. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close with no action, but the stock did not wait. **Nvidia closed down 14.01% at $125.53** on 607.8 million shares, about 2.6 times its three-month average volume. CNBC counted a seventh straight weekly decline, the longest since the 2008 financial crisis, and estimates of Friday's lost market value run around $431 billion.

Anthropic's second day as ANT went the other way from its debut. Reuters reported that Morgan Stanley, the offering's stabilization agent, closed its stabilizing position on Friday after exercising the full 147 million-share overallotment at the $83 IPO price, which lifts gross proceeds to about $93.5 billion but removes a standing buyer from the market. The shares sank to $83.05, five cents above the offer price, before recovering to close at **$88.91, down 8.5%** from Thursday's $97.17. Some investors questioned the bank stepping back while the stock was still 17% above its IPO price and technology shares were sliding.

Rates offered no cushion. Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the Fed should consider a half-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting, and futures price a December hike as a near certainty, with roughly 95% odds on a quarter point.

What comes next is a holiday-shortened week with little scheduled to change the mood. Nvidia has not addressed the Reuters report, and the governance story is still open, with its former chief executive due before House panels on December 1. For Anthropic, the test is whether the $83 level holds without Morgan Stanley's bid. For the broader market, a 10% weekly drop in the Nasdaq on a report about one company says how little conviction is left behind AI valuations after seven weeks of selling.

articles.title: Small open-weight models and Mac agents lead Friday's model news
body: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini on Friday with open weights under Apache 2.0, posting the model and a variable-loop research variant on Hugging Face. It is a mixture-of-experts model with **26.4 billion total parameters and 3.4 billion active**, and the design twist is a loop: the middle 12 layers run three times per token, adding computation without adding weights. The company says it fits on a laptop; coverage puts the footprint near 20 GB, enough for a 32 GB Apple silicon machine, a DGX Spark or a 32 GB GPU.

The lab's own numbers put it at 73.7% on SWE-bench Multilingual with only a bash tool, which it says leads small models on agentic coding; it also concedes weaker results in multi-turn chat and on instructions packed with constraints. The model is on the company's Tinker platform too. There is no independent evaluation yet.

Nvidia published a different kind of small model this week, with coverage on Friday. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a family of **14 checkpoints at 3B and 8B** under the Nvidia Nemotron Open Model License, which permits commercial use. Instead of producing one token at a time, it denoises token representations in a 16-dimensional embedding space and emits 64-token blocks, a continuous-diffusion approach; a self-speculative mode decodes about 3.46 times faster than Nvidia's autoregressive baseline, and the 8B base edges its earlier diffusion model on Nvidia's six-task suite.

On the agent side, Google turned on computer use in the Gemini Mac app on Thursday for US subscribers to AI Plus, Pro and Ultra, on **Apple silicon Macs running macOS 15 or later**. The agent works across local files, desktop apps and websites inside a live preview, so the user keeps the screen and cursor and can pause, stop or approve actions. Bloomberg noted that ChatGPT and Meta's Muse already offered similar Mac control, and reported that Apple is building its own agent that browses, codes and operates a Mac, possibly for late 2027, while tightening rules on apps that seek full disk access. OpenAI's Friday change was smaller: ChatGPT dictation now transcribes as you speak, and the 10-minute cap is gone on every plan.

None of the frontier labs shipped a new flagship on Friday, and that is the point. The movement is toward models small enough to run locally, decoding tricks that make them faster, and agents that act on the desktop a user already has. Apple's permission changes will shape how much room rivals have on the Mac before its own agent arrives, and independent benchmarks for Inkling 2 Mini and Sigma should land within days.

articles.title: Bitcoin breaks $60,000 as weekly ETF outflows top $1.2 billion
body: Bitcoin fell through $60,000 on Friday and kept sliding overnight. It traded near $58,700 by mid-afternoon Friday, down almost 6 percent on the day, and then dropped to about **$55,130 early Saturday**, its lowest level since September 2024, before bouncing back above $58,000. Crypto Times put the 24-hour decline near 10 percent, with more than $2.4 billion of leveraged positions liquidated across the market. Ether fell harder, trading around $1,638 on Friday.

The slide came in the worst week for US stocks since April 2025, with the S&P 500 in a correction and the Nasdaq negative for the year after Nvidia's 14 percent drop. Bitcoin had briefly rebounded toward $64,000 with tech stocks after Anthropic's IPO on Thursday; it gave all of that back within a day.

Fund flows kept pointing the same way. Thursday's $582 million net outflow, with a record $541 million leaving BlackRock's IBIT, was the heaviest day of the month. Farside's provisional tally for Friday showed about **$124.5 million** of net outflows from the other funds, with IBIT's own figure still blank as of Saturday morning. For the week of November 16 to 20 the spot bitcoin ETFs shed roughly $1.25 billion by one count, or $1.47 billion when ether funds are included, and IBIT alone lost close to $900 million. November is now near $3.5 billion of net outflows, the largest monthly exit since February.

The policy backdrop has stopped helping. CNBC argued Friday that the regulatory bull case has largely played out: the CLARITY market-structure bill stalled after the Senate failed to advance it in September, and the industry's remaining hopes rest on tokenization and new products rather than new law. Michael Saylor, whose Strategy sits on a paper loss on its 850,849 bitcoin, posted Friday that "Bitcoin is the foundation of everything we do at Strategy" as the company's shares fell.

What comes next is a test of the 2024 floor. Saturday's low leaves the September 2024 low near $54,592 as the next marker on the chart, while a daily close back above $60,000 would put the price back in the range it held in July. Weekend liquidity is thin, so the more telling numbers arrive Monday: IBIT's Friday flow, the first full-week tally, and whether a December Fed meeting at which markets price a rate increase keeps pressure on every risk asset at once.

articles.title: Tesla falls 7.6% as HSBC upgrade leans on SpaceX merger math
body: Tesla closed at **$345.82 on Friday, down 7.64 percent** from $374.41, one of the larger losers in a session that took the Nasdaq Composite down 5.3 percent. The drop came despite an upgrade from HSBC, where analyst Michael Tyndall moved the stock to Hold from Reduce and lifted his price target to $359 from $157.

The new target is almost entirely about a deal that has not been announced. Tyndall blends two scenarios: about $507 a share if SpaceX acquires Tesla at a 33 percent premium, and about $212 a share on standalone fundamentals. He sees little strategic logic in combining the two companies, which serve different customers, and assumes control is the real motive. Bloomberg reported on November 12 that the companies were in talks, with an announcement possible in December or early 2027; neither company has commented beyond Musk saying at DealBook that they would "probably" be better together.

On software, Musk wrote on X that FSD V15 goes to wide release next month and that "It will be something special." He answered yes when asked whether it would ship with the holiday update, which Tesla usually releases in mid-December, but gave no feature list and no word on which hardware generations are eligible. The current build in the 2026.44.1 update is FSD v14.3.13. V15 is the branch that is supposed to carry unsupervised operation for the Cybercab, whose first customer deliveries are estimated for December in Austin.

In Europe, Italy gave provisional approval on Friday to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name the supervised FSD system carries in the EU, with Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announcing the decision on X. Italy is the **12th EU country** to approve the system and the first of the bloc's four most populous members. It remains a Level 2 driver assist offered by subscription at 99 euros (about $109) a month; a December vote at the EU level needs at least 15 member states representing 65 percent of the population.

The HSBC note is useful mainly for what it says about the stock. If roughly $212 is a fair standalone value, then the gap to Friday's $345.82 close is merger premium, and Friday showed how quickly that premium can compress on a day when nothing about the deal changed. December now carries the shareholder meeting on the 3rd, the V15 release, the first Cybercab customer handovers, and the EU vote, any of which can move the stock as much as the merger headlines do.

articles.title: SpaceX flies USSF-317 as lenders balk at putting chips in orbit
body: A Falcon 9 lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg at **8:20 PM PT Friday** carrying the classified USSF-317 payload for the Space Force, after an unexplained Thursday scrub and roughly nine slips from a November 13 target. The first stage, on its 11th flight, landed on the drone ship Of Course I Still Love You about eight and a half minutes later. It was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of the year and SpaceX's third Space Force mission this month.

The stock had a worse day than the rocket. SPCX closed at **$127.79, down 7.69 percent** from $138.43, in the same rout that cost the Nasdaq 5.3 percent. The selling began premarket after SpaceX's roughly $32 billion bond sale priced with a top tranche yielding about 8.26 percent; the Saturn Funding structure behind it buys about $47.3 billion of Nvidia GPU equipment and leases it to SpaceX for about five years. The Financial Times reported that lenders asked for a clause barring those chips from orbital data centers, since hardware in orbit cannot be repossessed; it is unclear whether the clause survived. Flight 16 remains undated, with Ship 43's static fire not expected before mid-December.

Google, meanwhile, booked a competitor. Blue Origin said on November 19 that Google signed a launch agreement for a dedicated New Glenn mission for Project Suncatcher, targeting the first quarter of 2029, to deploy several satellites each carrying roughly a data center rack of TPU compute. Neither company disclosed the satellite count or price, and New Glenn has been grounded since a May test explosion, with return to flight slipped to January.

On the ground, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes asked Cochise County on November 19 to postpone a December 9 permit vote on SpaceX's proposed data center campus near Willcox, a $50 billion project on about 750 acres drawing up to **6 gigawatts**, close to a fifth of the state's current generating capacity. County board chair Frank Antenori said SpaceX has pledged to use no groundwater and to spend $3.6 billion on grid upgrades; the county has not verified those figures.

Orbital compute is being financed on terrestrial terms: SpaceX's lenders want collateral they can reach, Google wants a second launch provider, and Arizona wants to know who pays for 6 gigawatts. December 9 is now crowded, with the Cochise County vote, the Starbase tax abatement vote and the Fed meeting on the same day, while Flight 16 looks unlikely to fly before the year is out.

vocab.def: Of, relating to or happening in the evening; of flowers, opening in the evening; of animals, active or flying at dusk. The precise, slightly old-fashioned word for the hour after sunset, which this week arrives before 5 PM.

cards.b: From Latin vespertinus, from vesper, 'evening' or 'the evening star'. In English since the 1400s; the animal sense dates to about 1600. Related to Greek hesperos and to vespers, the evening church service
evening, dusky, twilight, crepuscular. Matutine is its morning twin; nocturnal is the whole night, not just its first hour
a walk you take at 5 PM in late November, moths and bats at the porch light, a flower like evening primrose that opens at dusk, the slow mood of a city after work

examples: The hike turned vespertine without anyone deciding it would; by the time we reached the car the ridge was a black line and the bay was lit up below us.
He kept vespertine hours all winter, saving the walk and the phone calls for the hour after the sun went down.
vocab.ex: The hike turned vespertine without anyone deciding it would; by the time we reached the car the ridge was a black line and the bay was lit up below us.

vocab.def: Having a strong religious or spiritual quality; suggesting the presence of something divine or awe-inspiring beyond ordinary understanding. Used of places, moments and works of art that stop you in your tracks.

cards.b: From Latin numen, 'a nod', then 'divine will, divine presence' (a god's nod of assent). Coined in English in the 1600s; given its modern sense by theologian Rudolf Otto in The Idea of the Holy (1917)
awe-inspiring, transcendent, sacred, otherworldly, holy. Not the same as noumenal (Kant's unknowable thing-in-itself), despite the look-alike spelling
a redwood grove at dawn, a cathedral you walked into by accident, the first clear night sky after a week of storms, the hush when a piece of music ends

examples: The fog burned off the ridge all at once, and for a minute the whole valley had a numinous quality nobody in the group tried to talk over.
She wasn't religious, but she called the old observatory numinous: the dome, the cold, the slow click of the clock drive.
vocab.ex: The fog burned off the ridge all at once, and for a minute the whole valley had a numinous quality nobody in the group tried to talk over.

vocab.def: The warmth of the sun in winter; the feeling of sunshine on a cold day. A rare, nearly obsolete word first recorded in English in 1623.

cards.b: From Latin apricus, 'warmed by the sun, sunny' (apricari, 'to bask in the sun'); the same root gives 'apricot' by way of a folk etymology
winter sunshine, sun-warmth; no exact single-word synonym, which is why people keep reviving it. Opposite idea: chill, rawness
the first clear afternoon after a storm, a cold morning on a sunny bench, the patch of sun a cat finds in December

examples: After two days of rain the clouds broke around three, and the whole office drifted outside for ten minutes of apricity.
The trail was still muddy, but the apricity on the ridge made the climb feel like a reward.
vocab.ex: After two days of rain the clouds broke around three, and the whole office drifted outside for ten minutes of apricity.

vocab.def: Of or relating to rain; marked by heavy or abundant rainfall. In geology, a pluvial is a long wet period in a region's climate history.

cards.b: From Latin pluvia, 'rain' (pluere, 'to rain'); the same root gives Spanish lluvia and French pluie
rainy, wet, sodden; the technical cousin of 'drizzly' and 'monsoonal'. Antonym: arid
a storm day like this one, a wet winter, a region's rainy season, or a lake that filled during an ancient wet epoch

examples: The whole Peninsula went pluvial overnight: creeks up, lights out, the bike lane a river.
Lake Lahontan is a ghost of the last pluvial, when Nevada was wet enough to hold an inland sea.
vocab.ex: The whole Peninsula went pluvial overnight: creeks up, lights out, the bike lane a river.

vocab.def: A clumsy, inelegant fix that works anyway: a solution bolted together from mismatched parts because it had to ship today.

cards.b: Engineering slang popularized by Jackson Granholm's 1962 Datamation essay 'How to Design a Kludge'; often traced to German klug ('clever') or Scots cludgie, though the origin is disputed
hack, workaround, bodge, duct-tape fix, Rube Goldberg machine; the opposite of an elegant design
a zip-tied cable harness that shipped, the regex that parses a log file nobody will ever touch again, a hotfix with a TODO from 2023 still in it

examples: The gripper timing was a kludge, a 40-millisecond sleep nobody could explain, and it held through the whole demo.
Every lab has one kludge it is secretly proud of, and it is usually load-bearing.
vocab.ex: The gripper timing was a kludge, a 40-millisecond sleep nobody could explain, and it held through the whole demo.

vocab.def: Studied carelessness: the art of making something difficult look effortless, hiding all the work that went into it.

cards.b: Italian, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in The Book of the Courtier (1528) for the grace of a courtier who never seems to be trying
nonchalance, effortless grace, understated mastery; the opposite of visible strain or showing your work
a demo that looks easy because of three weeks of tuning, a chef plating without looking, an open-collar suit that took an hour

examples: The demo had real sprezzatura: the robot folded the shirt like an afterthought, and nobody saw the 400 failed runs behind it.
His slides have a kind of sprezzatura, four words a page and not a hint of the late nights that produced them.
vocab.ex: The demo had real sprezzatura: the robot folded the shirt like an afterthought, and nobody saw the 400 failed runs behind it.

vocab.def: A manuscript page that was scraped clean and written over, with traces of the old text still showing; by extension, anything that carries visible layers of its earlier versions.

cards.b: Greek palin ('again') + psēstos ('scraped'): parchment was expensive, so monks scraped off old texts and reused the skin
layered record, overwritten text, accretion; near relatives: patina, sediment, legacy code
a city block with 1920s brick behind a glass facade, a codebase where every refactor left fossils, a face that shows every earlier age

examples: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.
Downtown is a palimpsest of booms, with the cannery brick, the dot-com stucco and the new glass all on one block.
vocab.ex: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.

spanish.meaning: That's it, it's ruined; we're done for; it's had it
spanish.note: Literally 'it was already worth', which makes no sense, and that's the point: in Mexican Spanish ya valió is the set phrase for the moment a plan collapses, a thing breaks for good or trouble is walking toward you. A linguistics paper from El Colegio de México lists it among the fixed expressions built on ya, next to ya mero. It's mild on its own; the stronger versions add madre or another swear word and are vulgar, so stop at ya valió, or use the jokey softeners ya valió gorro or ya valió queso. Say it about a thing (la lavadora ya valió), a plan (el picnic ya valió) or the whole situation (¡ya valió!).

cards.es: Se puso a llover y ya valió el plan
cards.en: It started raining and that's the plan ruined

cards.es: Mi celular se cayó al agua. Ya valió.
cards.en: My phone fell in the water. It's done for.

cards.es: Viene el jefe. Ya valió, muchachos.
cards.en: The boss is coming. We're done for, guys.

parts.en: already, now; here it marks that the thing just became true
was worth (preterite of valer); in the idiom, it means the opposite: it's worthless now
same thing, jokey softener (gorro means cap)
same thing, even sillier softener
oh well, nothing to be done; what you say right after
it got spoiled, it went bad; the neutral way to say it

dialog.es: ¿Siempre sí vamos al cerro mañana?
dialog.en: Are we still going up the hill tomorrow?

dialog.es: Dicen que va a llover todo el domingo. Ya valió.
dialog.en: They say it's going to rain all Sunday. That's that, then.

dialog.es: Ni modo. ¿Entonces qué, pelis y tacos?
dialog.en: Oh well. So what, movies and tacos?

dialog.es: Sale. Pero los tacos los pagas tú.
dialog.en: Deal. But you're buying the tacos.

spanish.use: Say it with a sigh the moment tonight's rain shows up on the radar, then follow it with ni modo and a plan B; it's the most Mexican way to shrug off a wrecked plan.

spanish.meaning: I'm totally broke; I'm out of money
spanish.note: Bruja means witch, but in Mexican slang estar or andar bruja means to have no money, and bien is the all-purpose intensifier that turns broke into flat broke. Nobody is sure where it comes from; the Mexican proverb collections just record it as a colloquial way to say you're skint. It's light and self-mocking, the kind of thing you say when friends propose a plan you can't afford this week, and it works for anyone regardless of gender: a man still says ando bruja, not brujo. The polite alternative is no tengo dinero or ando corto, but bruja is what you'll actually hear.

cards.es: Ando bien bruja hasta la quincena
cards.en: I'm flat broke until payday

cards.es: ¿Vamos al concierto? No, ando bruja
cards.en: Should we go to the concert? No, I'm broke

cards.es: Después del viaje quedé bien bruja
cards.en: After the trip I ended up totally broke

parts.en: I'm going around, I am (andar used like estar for states)
very, really; the Mexican intensifier (bien bueno, bien caro)
witch; in slang, broke, penniless (always the feminine form)
payday, the twice-monthly paycheck
I'm short (on cash), the milder version
money (literally wool); another slang word you'll hear with it

dialog.es: ¿Vamos por unos tacos y luego al bar?
dialog.en: Should we go get tacos and then hit the bar?

dialog.es: Tacos sí, bar no. Ando bien bruja.
dialog.en: Tacos yes, bar no. I'm totally broke.

dialog.es: ¿Otra vez? ¿Pues en qué gastas?
dialog.en: Again? What do you spend it on?

spanish.meaning: Almost; just about; any minute now
spanish.note: Mero is a Mexican all-purpose intensifier, and ya mero is how you say something is almost done, almost here or almost true. Ya mero llego means I'm almost there, which in practice can mean anywhere from two minutes to twenty. Said with a rising tone and a question mark, ¿ya mero? means 'almost done?' or 'are we there yet?'. It is friendlier and vaguer than casi, which makes it the natural answer when someone asks how much longer.

spanish.meaning: I'm going to take a quick nap

dare.title: See the maples turn at Hakone
dare.why: Late November is when the Japanese maples at Hakone Estate and Gardens in Saratoga go red all at once, and today is the dry, soft-light day to catch them before tonight's rain knocks the leaves down. Winter hours are 11 AM to 4 PM on weekends with last entry at 3 PM, adults are $12 at the gate, and it's about 25 minutes down Highway 85 and Big Basin Way from you, so go when the gate opens and you'll have the hill-and-pond garden nearly to yourself. The one rule: do a full slow lap of the pond, the bamboo path and the moon bridge before you take a single photo.
dare.worth: It's an 18-acre hillside garden laid out in 1915, one of the oldest Japanese-style gardens in the Western Hemisphere, and in peak color it feels like a different country for the price of a sandwich. Fall color here lasts about ten days a year, so seeing it is the kind of thing you remember the exact year of.

swap.title: Press the best leaf on your street
swap.why: Walk your own block, pick the single best fallen leaf you can find (color beats size), flatten it between two sheets of paper inside the heaviest book you own, and write today's date in pencil on the page. Ten minutes, no driving, and the rain tonight means today is the last good day for it.
swap.worth: In a month it's a bookmark that holds a specific November afternoon, and you'll have actually looked at the trees you walk past every day.
